edges.description: The thirteen mtDNA-encoded subunits are distributed across complexes I, III, IV and V, so under-supplying them makes those complexes fail together while complex II, wholly nuclear-encoded, is spared.
Glycolytic compensation converts accumulating pyruvate to lactate.
Cardiomyocytes depend on oxidative phosphorylation, and cardiomyopathy is the most frequently reported manifestation.
The developing and mature nervous system has high oxidative demand; neurological involvement ranges from neonatal encephalomyopathy to juvenile Leigh syndrome and movement disorder.
Neonatal liver failure is reported in a homozygous p.Arg333Trp (R312W) family.
The alternative morphology, reported in the adult patient with fibro-adipose replacement.

edges.description: Patient fibroblasts show the joint loss of EF-Ts and EF-Tu and reduced assembly of complexes I, IV and V, and retroviral EF-Ts or EF-Tu corrects it.
edges.limitations: Fibroblasts are not an affected tissue, and in at least one patient they compensated by up-regulating EF-Tu and mitochondrial biogenesis and had normal oxygen consumption while her heart was severely deficient. The size of the defect in fibroblasts is therefore not a guide to severity in heart, brain or liver.

nodes.description: Biallelic TSFM variants reduce the amount or activity of EF-Ts. The recurrent p.Arg333Trp substitution lies in the subdomain that contacts EF-Tu and weakens EF-Tu binding, so nucleotide exchange on EF-Tu is impaired; other coding alleles destabilise EF-Ts so that it is absent from patient cells. Either way the cell has less capacity to recharge EF-Tu with GTP between rounds of aminoacyl-tRNA delivery.

nodes.description: With the mtDNA-dependent complexes under-assembled, cells cannot meet ATP demand by oxidative phosphorylation and shift to glycolysis. The organs that fail are those with the highest and least flexible oxidative demand: heart, brain and, in the neonatal period, liver. Why one patient's disease is cardiac and another's is neurological or hepatic is not explained; the founding authors invoked genetic modifiers because the same homozygous allele produced different organ involvement.

nodes.description: Assembled complexes I, IV and V are reduced in patient fibroblasts, and patient myocardium shows reduced complex I and IV activity with complex II, III and V subunits preserved. Muscle biopsy in other patients shows multiple respiratory chain deficiency or a predominant complex IV defect. Which complex falls furthest varies with tissue and patient, as expected for a translation defect that touches all four mtDNA-dependent complexes. Complex II sparing has been shown at the subunit level in heart and by normal succinate dehydrogenase histochemistry in skeletal muscle.

nodes.description: The steady-state levels of both EF-Ts and its partner EF-Tu fall in patient cells and in affected myocardium. Loss of EF-Tu as well as EF-Ts is why retroviral expression of either factor can rescue patient fibroblasts, and it means the defect is not only slower nucleotide exchange but a smaller pool of the factor that delivers aminoacyl-tRNA to the ribosome. In one patient the fibroblasts compensated by raising EF-Tu while the heart did not, which is offered as an explanation for tissue selectivity.
